1.goal: To open the lesson on who sees her numbers outside Brazil, to find out whether she has started at the US company, and to tell her what the lesson ends with.
run: Ask whether she did the pre-class and whether anything in it was unclear.
Tell her what the lesson ends with, in one sentence: she presents the cost of a turnover problem to leaders in the US, twice.
Ask the question on screen. If she does not mention the US company, ask about it.
exact: What today is: “Today you present what turnover costs, in dollars, to leaders in the US. Then you do it again with a new figure.”
About the US company: “Have you started at the new company yet? Who will you report to there?”
1.expected: One or two people or roles, and a sentence about the US company if it applies. A complete answer looks like “My boss in the US and the regional finance team. I start at the new company next month.” Any answer is right here; note what she says about the new company.
1.support: If she has no one in mind, ask who saw her reports at her last company.
1.challenge: Ask what that person usually asks her first about a number.
1.monitoring: Whether she mentions dollars or people first.
1.evidence: What she said about the US company, in her words.
1.transition: Move on when she has answered.

2.goal: To set the real-world objective: her role, who is listening, what they know, and the result she wants.
2.interaction: T–S, reading the brief on screen together.
run: Read the brief with her.
Ask the question on screen and let her answer in one sentence.
2.expected: Either answer can be defended; what matters is the reason. A complete answer looks like “How many people left, because the dollars only make sense after that.” or “The dollars, because the CFO thinks in money.”
2.support: If she hesitates, ask what the CFO would ask first if she started with dollars.
2.challenge: Ask what would make the VP of HR and the CFO want different things from the same presentation.
2.monitoring: Whether she thinks about the listener or about her own material.
2.transition: Move on when she has answered with a reason.

3.goal: To see how she presents a cost today, before any model, with the case she chooses.
3.interaction: S–T, spoken. You are the CFO; you listen and ask one question at the end.
run: Read the two options with her and let her choose. For option B, give her a moment to decide her numbers.
Let her present without interrupting. Leave corrections for screen 9.
Write down one sentence with a number, word for word. At the end, ask one question.
exact: Your question at the end: “Where does the $4,870 come from?” (option A) / “How did you get to that total?” (option B)
3.expected: There is no answer key on this screen: it is the version she has today. For option A, a complete attempt includes the 71 exits, the cost per exit, a total and the request, for example “We had 71 people leaving in the second quarter, and each exit costs around $4,870, so it is more or less $346,000. I would like $120,000 for a pilot.” Note the order of the information and how the total comes out.
3.support: If she stops early, point at the next line in her option.
3.challenge: Ask how much of the total is money the company actually paid.
3.monitoring: Whether the total is rounded or exact, and whether the calculation comes with it.
3.evidence: One sentence with a number, word for word. It goes into the third board on screen 9.
3.transition: Move on when she has presented and answered your question.

4.goal: To compare her attempt with a short model, and to notice what the model does with the numbers.
run: Read the question on screen with her.
Play the five sentences once, in order.
Ask the two parts of the question: what was also in her version, and what the model does differently with the numbers.
exact: Before pressing Play: “Listen to all five. Then tell me what was also in yours, and what is different.”
4.expected: Parts that are usually in both: the number of people, the cost per exit, the total, the request. What the model does differently: it says what the number is before the number (“We lost 71 people”), gives the rounded total first (“roughly $346,000”) and the exact figure in a separate sentence (“$345,770, to be exact”), and separates lost productivity from cash (“about $2,800 per person, is lost productivity, not cash”). Anything she names that is in the five sentences is correct.
4.support: If she says “it is clearer”, ask which sentence made it clearer.
4.challenge: Ask which sentence of the model she would say differently, and how.
4.monitoring: Whether she compares at the level of the numbers or only the general impression.
4.evidence: What she noticed without being prompted.
4.transition: Move on when she has named at least one thing the model does with the numbers.

5.goal: To classify what each sentence of the model does for the CFO.
5.interaction: S alone on the activity, then T–S.
run: Let her classify the five sentences and press Check.
Go through them. On the two total sentences, ask why the model gives the total twice.
exact: On the two total sentences: “Why does the presenter say the total twice?”
5.expected: Says what happened: “We lost 71 people across the two sites in the second quarter.” Gives the total, or how it was reached: “At about $4,870 each, that comes to roughly $346,000.” · “$345,770, to be exact.” Separates cash from lost value: “Most of it, about $2,800 per person, is lost productivity, not cash.” Asks for a decision: “What I am asking for is $120,000 for a six-month pilot of a new shift model.” The total is said twice: rounded first so it can be kept, exact after for anyone who needs it.
5.support: On each sentence, ask what the CFO has after hearing it that they did not have before.
5.challenge: Ask which job is missing from her own version on screen 3.
5.monitoring: Whether she sees the function of each sentence or classifies by the words.
5.evidence: Which job she said was missing from her own version, if she said one.
5.transition: Move on when the five are classified.

6.goal: To have her find what makes a total easy to keep after one hearing, before the reveal.
run: Read the two versions out loud, at normal speed, and ask the question on screen.
Let her answer before you open the button.
Open what makes the difference and read it with her.
exact: If she does not see it: “After version 1, tell me the total. After version 2, tell me the total.”
6.expected: Version 2. From the reveal: one number per sentence, what the number is before the number, and the rounded total first, with the exact figure after it if it matters. In version 1 the total arrives exact, at the end of a long sentence, after another number.
6.support: Read version 1 again and ask her to repeat the total without looking.
6.challenge: Ask her to say the Campinas total in the version 2 shape.
6.monitoring: Whether she finds the pattern before the reveal.
6.evidence: Her own words for what makes the difference.
6.transition: Move on when the reveal has been read.

7.goal: To practice saying the figures of the case in the order that works by ear: what it is, rounded, exact.
7.interaction: T–S, spoken, one figure at a time.
run: Point at one row of the table at a time.
She says what it is, the rounded number, and the exact number.
On the row with three parts, ask her to say how much is cash and how much is lost productivity.
exact: Pointing at a row: “This one. What is it, roughly, and exactly?”
7.expected: Campinas: “The Campinas exits cost roughly $112,000. $112,010, to be exact.” Guarulhos: “roughly $234,000; $233,760, to be exact.” One exit: “Of about $4,870, $2,070 is cash — recruiting and training — and $2,800 is lost productivity.” The pilot: “$120,000 over six months, which is $20,000 a month.” Numbers said in full, for example two hundred thirty-three thousand seven hundred sixty dollars.
7.support: If a number stalls, say what it is and the first word of the number, and let her finish.
7.challenge: Ask for the total of the two sites in the same shape without looking at the screen.
7.monitoring: Which numbers she says in full and which she rounds to avoid.
7.evidence: The figures that stalled, if any.
7.transition: Move on when the four rows have been said.

8.goal: To present the case in full to the VP of HR and the CFO, answering questions she did not prepare for.
8.interaction: Simulation, round one. You are the VP of HR and the CFO; she presents.
run: Read the task and the list on screen with her. She presents the case she chose on screen 3.
Let her give what happened and the total. Then ask the first question below; later, the second; at the end, the third.
Wait for a check when a question can mean two things. The sentence starters stay closed; open them only if she stops. Leave corrections for screen 9, and write down one sentence with a number.
exact: As the CFO: “Is that a lot?”
As the VP of HR: “How sure are you about the $4,870?” (option A) / “Where does the cost per exit come from?” (option B)
As the CFO, at the end: “And when would the pilot pay for itself?”
8.expected: The presentation in the order of the list, and three answers. For option A: what happened (71 exits in the second quarter, 48 and 23), the total rounded first with the calculation, and the request of $120,000. To “Is that a lot?”, a check first (“Compared with what: last year, or the pilot?”), then an answer to the meaning you choose. To the second question, that it is an estimate, with its parts ($1,150 recruiting, $920 training, $2,800 lost productivity). The third question has no fixed answer; a complete answer marks it as her reading, for example “If the pilot cut exits by a third, it would save roughly $115,000 a quarter, so it would pay for itself in about one quarter — but that depends on the result.” For option B the figures are hers; the check is the same shape.
8.support: If she answers “Is that a lot?” without checking, ask it again the same way and wait.
8.challenge: Add a question she has not heard: “Why not just pay people more?”
8.monitoring: The order of the information, the shape of the total, the check before the ambiguous question, and what happens to her English after the third question.
8.evidence: One sentence with a number, word for word, and whether she checked “Is that a lot?”.
8.transition: Move on when she has presented and answered the three questions.

9.goal: To name what worked and what held up under questions, and to upgrade one sentence with a number.
run: Write one thing that worked in round one, and one point to improve. Take the point from what happened, not from a list.
Write her sentence from screen 3 or screen 8 in the third box, as she said it.
Build the upgraded version with her in the fourth box, in the shape from screen 6, and ask her to say it.
exact: Building the upgrade: “What is the number first? Now the rounded figure. Now, if it matters, the exact one.”
9.expected: Four filled boards. A typical upgrade: from “We had 71 people leaving and it is more or less three hundred and forty-five thousand seven hundred seventy dollars” to “We lost 71 people in the second quarter. That comes to roughly $346,000.” If round one was already clean, the point to improve can be a strength to keep under more pressure, for example the check before answering.
9.support: If she cannot choose a sentence, use the one you wrote down on screen 3.
9.challenge: Ask her to say the upgraded sentence and add the request in one more sentence.
9.monitoring: Whether she can say the upgraded sentence without reading it.
9.evidence: The sentence as she said it and the upgraded version.
9.transition: Move on when the upgraded sentence has been said out loud.

10.goal: To present the case again with a changed figure and a new listener, saying what changed and whether the request stays.
10.interaction: Simulation, round two, a new task: the cost per exit changes and the CEO joins. You are the CEO.
run: Read the two cards with her: what she presented in round one, and what Finance sent.
Open as the CEO with the first question below. Let her present with the new figure.
Ask the second question when she gives the request. Leave corrections for later.
exact: As the CEO, opening: “I only have a minute. What is the total?”
As the CEO, on the request: “The cost went up. Do you need more money for the pilot now?”
10.expected: The new total first, rounded: “Roughly $378,000. $377,720, to be exact.” Then what changed and why, with the verb for the period: “Since the last version, the cost per exit has gone up to about $5,320, because recruiting fees went up with a new agency contract.” To the second question: the pilot cost stays the same, $120,000; a complete answer says why, for example “No. The pilot still costs $120,000. The higher cost per exit makes it pay for itself sooner.” For option B the figures are hers, with a changed cost per exit of her choice.
10.support: If she uses the old total, point at the card from Finance and wait.
10.challenge: Ask her to say how much more the problem costs now than in round one: roughly $32,000.
10.monitoring: Whether the new figure replaces the old one, and whether the present perfect comes with “since the last version”.
10.evidence: What changed from round one to round two in the shape of the total and in her answers. It closes the block.
10.transition: Move on when she has given the new total and answered about the request.

11.goal: To close the lesson and the block on what was worked on, let her say how confident she feels, and leave the homework said out loud.
11.interaction: T–S, going through the recap and the confidence scale together.
run: Go through the recap list with her and tick what was done.
Let her fill the confidence scale herself.
Read the three lines on the right and say the homework out loud.
exact: The homework, said out loud: “This week, when you give a number to someone, say what it is first, then the rounded figure.”
11.expected: The recap has seven lines, and all seven were done if the lesson ran to the end: presenting before the model, comparing with the model, saying what a number is before the number, rounded before exact, cash and lost value, answering unprepared questions with a check, and presenting again with a new figure. The confidence scale is hers, and it may come out lower than what you saw.
11.support: If she marks everything low, read her upgraded sentence from screen 9.
11.challenge: Ask which of the four lessons of the block she would use first at work, and where.
11.monitoring: Whether her self-assessment matches what you observed across the four lessons.
11.evidence: Her confidence marks, and what she said about the block.
11.transition: End here. The next block starts from what these four lessons showed.
